# P14.8 v4 — exact reconstruction dichotomy

Let $X$ be a connected compact Kähler manifold, and let $\theta$ be a smooth
closed real $(1,1)$-form such that $\operatorname{PSH}(X,\theta)\ne\varnothing$.
Write

$$
\mathscr D_{\mathcal I}(X,\theta)
:=\operatorname{PSH}(X,\theta)/{\sim_{\mathcal I}}
$$

for the set of *realizable* $\mathcal I$-data. Thus an element is induced by
an actual $\varphi\in\operatorname{PSH}(X,\theta)$ and is represented by the
tower $(\mathcal I(m\varphi))_{m\ge1}$, equivalently by its divisorial Lelong
profile; it is not an arbitrary formal sequence of ideals. For
$d=[\varphi]_{\mathcal I}$, define

$$
\mathcal R_\theta(d):=P_\theta[\varphi]_{\mathcal I}.
$$

**Theorem (P14.8 v4).**

1. The map $\mathcal R_\theta$ is well defined and returns the unique
   normalized $\mathcal I$-model potential in the class $d$. Hence full
   realizable $\mathcal I$-data reconstructs its canonical normalized
   $\mathcal I$-model representative, with no hypothesis on nonpluripolar
   mass.

2. Raw nonpluripolar mass is not part of $\mathcal I$-data. On
   $X=\mathbf P^1$, equipped with the Fubini--Study form $\omega$ normalized
   by $\int_X\omega=1$, there is one $\mathcal I$-class containing potentials
   $\varphi_s$, $0\le s\le1$, such that

   $$
   [\varphi_s]_{\mathcal I}=[0]_{\mathcal I},\qquad
   \int_X\left\langle\omega+\operatorname{dd}^c\varphi_s\right\rangle=1-s.
   $$

   In particular, the raw zero-mass representative $\varphi_1$ has canonical
   normalized $\mathcal I$-model representative $0$, whose mass is one. So
   neither a raw zero-mass representative nor its mass can be reconstructed
   from its $\mathcal I$-class.

These settle the two defined readings of the former P14.8 wording: complete
realizable $\mathcal I$-data determines the canonical normalized
$\mathcal I$-model representative, while neither a raw representative nor
its raw mass descends to the $\mathcal I$-quotient.

**Scope.** On a smooth projective variety, the separate all-mass order
isomorphism for full realized DXZ--Boucksom--Jonsson objects in a
pseudoeffective real Néron--Severi class remains distinct. The literal
all-semivaluation ideal formula is used only for a $\mathbf Q$-line-bundle
class. This theorem asserts neither a compact-Kähler nor a genuinely
transcendental extension of that result. Realization of arbitrary formal
ideal or valuative data remains P14.1, and the P14.7 terminal-left-limit
corollary is not used here.

## Interfaces used

1. Boucksom, Lemma 2.6: for an increasing sequence of psh functions
   converging almost everywhere to a psh limit, point Lelong numbers decrease
   to the Lelong number of the limit. Boucksom, Lemma 10.5 permits a very
   general point of a prime divisor to compute each generic Lelong number in a
   countable family. Together with Choquet's lemma, these give the
   increasing-envelope step in the proof.

2. Boucksom, Corollary 10.18: multiplier-ideal membership is characterized
   by the divisorial Lelong profile and log discrepancies. Applying it to
   every positive integral scaling shows that equal divisorial profiles give
   equal multiplier-ideal towers. Conversely, the analytic-approximation
   inequalities used in the proof of Theorem 10.13 give the correct
   discrepancy-dependent squeeze
   $\nu_E(\varphi)\ge m^{-1}\operatorname{ord}_E\mathcal I(m\varphi)
   \ge\nu_E(\varphi)-A(E)/m$; equality of the full towers therefore gives
   equality of profiles.

3. BEGZ, Section 1.2 and Proposition 1.4: the degree-one nonpluripolar
   product is well-defined, local where the potential is locally bounded, and
   gives no mass to pluripolar sets. Those are the only nonpluripolar-product
   properties used in the curve computation.

4. The generalized-Cantor logarithmic-capacity criterion used in the explicit
   construction is the classical criterion cited in the candidate as
   Carleson, *Selected Problems on Exceptional Sets*, p. 31. The proof uses
   only the displayed divergence calculation and the resulting polarity.

## Deliberate exclusions

This packet does **not** use a pointwise $n/m$ estimate for divisorial
valuations, global truncation positivity for arbitrary smooth backgrounds,
levelwise truncation multilinearity or closedness, unrestricted mixed-mass
monotonicity, or a one-sided $\mathcal I$-preorder equivalence. Those were
the unrelated defective supporting claims in the rejected v3 dependency.

                 3. Regularization of quasi-psh functions
3.1. Quasi-psh functions and singular metrics. As mentioned above, psh
functions make sense on any complex manifold X.
Definition 3.1. A usc function φ : X → [−∞, +∞) on a complex manifold X
is quasi-psh if it is locally of the form φ = u + f where u is psh and f is smooth.
   It will be convenient to introduce the real operator ddc := πi ∂∂ (the role of the
normalization factor π will become apparent below). By the Poincaré lemma,
any closed, real (1, 1)-form θ on X is locally of the form θ = ddc f for a smooth
real-valued function f , called a local potential of θ. In particular, θ is a Kähler
form if and only if its local potentials are strictly psh.
Definition 3.2. A quasi-psh function φ is θ-psh if θ + ddc φ ≥ 0 in the sense of
currents; equivalently, f + φ is (locally) psh for any choice of local potentials f
for θ.
   Let now L be a Hermitian holomorphic line bundle on X. The curvature form
of L is the closed, real (1, 1)-form θ locally defined by θ := −ddc log |τ | for any
local trivializing (holomorphic) section τ of L. This (1, 1)-form is indeed globally
well-defined, as any other local trivializing section is of the form τ ′ = uτ with
u ∈ O⋆X , and ddc log |τ ′ | = ddc log |τ | since log |u| pluriharmonic.
   This definition of the curvature form θ is simply a concrete description of the
curvature form of the Chern connection of L, normalized so that θ represents
                       SINGULARITIES AND MULTIPLIER IDEALS                           11

the first Chern class of L in de Rham cohomology, i.e. the image in H 2 (X, R) of
c1 (L) ∈ H 2 (X, Z).
    Any other Hermitian metric on L is of the form | · |′ = | · |e−φ with φ ∈ C ∞ (X),
and the curvature forms are related by θ′ = θ + ddc φ. The data of a θ-psh
function φ can thus be interpreted as that of a singular metric | · |e−φ on L with
semipositive curvature current θ + ddc φ.

                                                Abstract. We deﬁne non-pluripolar products of an arbitrary number of
                                                closed positive (1, 1)-currents on a compact Kähler manifold X. Given a
                                                big (1, 1)-cohomology class α on X (i.e. a class that can be represented by
                                                a strictly positive current) and a positive measure µ on X of total mass equal
                                                to the volume of α and putting no mass on pluripolar sets, we show that µ
                                                can be written in a unique way as the top degree self-intersection in the non-
                                                pluripolar sense of a closed positive current in α. We then extend Kolodziedj’s
                                                approach to sup-norm estimates to show that the solution has minimal singu-
                                                larities in the sense of Demailly if µ has L1+ε -density with respect to Lebesgue
                                                measure. If µ is smooth and positive everywhere, we prove that T is smooth
                                                on the ample locus of α provided α is nef. Using a ﬁxed point theorem we
                                                ﬁnally explain how to construct singular Kähler-Einstein volume forms with
                                                minimal singularities on varieties of general type.

                                   Introduction
  The primary goal of the present paper is to extend the results obtained by
the last two authors on complex Monge-Ampère equations on compact Kähler
manifolds in [31] to the case of arbitrary cohomology classes.
  More speciﬁcally let X be a compact n-dimensional Kähler manifold and let
ω be a Kähler form on X. An ω-plurisubharmonic (psh for short) function is an
upper semi-continuous function ϕ such that ω + ddc ϕ is positive in the sense of
currents, and [31] focused on the Monge-Ampère type equation
                                   (ω + ddc ϕ)n = µ                              (0.1)

where µ is a positive measure on X of total mass µ(X) = X ω n . As is well-
known, it is not always possible to make sense of the left-hand side of (0.1),
but it was observed in [31] that a construction going back to Bedford-Taylor [4]
enables in this global setting to deﬁne the non-pluripolar part of the would-be
positive measure (ω + ddc ϕ)n for an arbitrary ω-psh function ϕ.
  In the present paper we ﬁrst give a more systematic treatment of these issues.
We explain how to deﬁne in a simple and canonical way the non-pluripolar product

Theorem B. Assume that the measure µ in Theorem A furthermore has L1+ε

to hT n i = µ has minimal singularities.
   Currents with minimal singularities were introduced by Demailly. When α is
a Kähler class, the positive currents T ∈ α with minimal singularities are exactly
those with locally bounded potentials. When α is merely big all positive currents
T ∈ α will have poles in general, and the minimal singularity condition on T
essentially says that T has the least possible poles among all positive currents
in α. Currents with minimal singularities have in particular locally bounded
potentials on the ample locus Amp (α) of α, which is roughly speaking the largest
Zariski open subset where α locally looks like a Kähler class.
   Regarding local regularity properties, we obtain the following result.
Theorem C. In the setting of Theorem A, assume that µ is a smooth strictly
positive volume form. Assume also that α is nef. Then the solution T ∈ α to the
equation hT n i = µ is C ∞ on Amp (α).

  In this section X denotes an arbitrary n-dimensional complex manifold unless
otherwise speciﬁed.

1.1. Plurifine topology. The plurifine topology on X is deﬁned as the coarsest
topology with respect to which all psh functions u on all open subsets of X become
continuous (cf. [4]). Note that the pluriﬁne topology on X is always strictly ﬁner
than the ordinary one.
   Since psh functions are upper semi-continuous, subsets of the form
                                       V ∩ {u > 0}
with V ⊂ X open and u psh on V obviously form a basis for the pluriﬁne topology,
and u can furthermore be assumed to be locally bounded by maxing it with 0.
  When X is furthermore compact and Kähler, a bounded local psh function
deﬁned on an open subset V of X can be extended to a quasi-psh function on X
(possibly after shrinking V a little bit, see [30]), and it follows that the pluriﬁne
topology on X can alternatively be described as the coarsest topology with respect
to which all bounded and quasi-psh functions ϕ on X become continuous. It
therefore admits sets of the form V ∩ {ϕ > 0} with V ⊂ X open and ϕ quasi-psh
and bounded on X as a basis.

1.3. Positive cohomology classes. Let X be a compact Kähler manifold and
let α ∈ H 1,1 (X, R) be a real (1, 1)-cohomology class.
   Recall that α is said to be pseudo-effective (psef for short) if it can be repre-
sented by a closed positive (1, 1)-current T . If θ is a given smooth representative
of α, then any such current can be written as T = θ + ddc ϕ, where ϕ is thus a θ-
psh function by deﬁnition, and will sometimes be referred to as a global potential
of T . Global potentials only depend on the choice of θ up to a smooth function
on X.
   On the other hand, α is nef if it lies in the closure of the Kähler cone. Such
a class can thus be represented by smooth forms with arbitrarily small nega-
tive parts, and a compactness argument then shows that α contains a positive
current, i.e. nef implies psef. Note however that the negative part of smooth
representatives cannot be taken to be 0 in general. In fact, Demailly, Peternell
and Schneider have shown in [23] that a classical construction of Serre yields an
example of a smooth curve C on a projective surface whose cohomology class is
nef but contains only one positive current, to wit (the integration current on) C
itself.
   The set of all nef classes is by deﬁnition a closed convex cone in H 1,1 (X, R),
whose interior is none but the Kähler cone. The set of all psef classes also forms a
closed convex cone, and its interior is by deﬁnition the set of all big cohomology
classes. In other words, a class α is big iﬀ it can be represented by a strictly
positive current, i.e. a closed current T that dominates some (small enough)
smooth strictly positive form on X.

1.4. Comparison of singularities. If T and T ′ are two closed positive currents
on X, then T is said to be more singular than T ′ if their global potentials satisfy
ϕ ≤ ϕ′ + O(1). By the singularity type of T , we will mean its equivalence class
with respect to the above notion of comparison of singularities.
   A positive current T in a given psef class α is now said to have minimal
singularities (inside its cohomology class) if it is less singular than any other
positive current in α, and its θ-psh potentials ϕ will correspondingly be said
to have minimal singularities. Such θ-psh functions with minimal singularities
always exist, as was observed by Demailly. Indeed, the upper envelope
                         Vθ := sup {ϕ θ-psh, ϕ ≤ 0 on X}
of all non-positive θ-psh functions obviously yields a positive current
                                     θ + ddc Vθ
with minimal singularities (note that Vθ is usc since Vθ∗ is a candidate in the
envelope).
   We stress that currents with minimal singularities in a given class α are in
general far from unique. Indeed currents with minimal singularities in a class
α admitting a smooth non-negative representative θ ≥ 0 (for instance a Kähler

# P14.8 v4 — proof

Fix $d=[\varphi]_{\mathcal I}$ and set

$$
\mathcal F_d:=\{\psi\in\operatorname{PSH}(X,\theta):
  \psi\le0,\ [\psi]_{\mathcal I}=d\}.
$$

This family is nonempty, since $\varphi-\sup_X\varphi\in\mathcal F_d$. It is
directed under finite maxima. The source package identifies the full
multiplier-ideal tower with its divisorial profile using the
discrepancy-dependent approximation, and generic Lelong numbers satisfy

$$
\nu(\max\{\psi_1,\psi_2\},E)=
\min\{\nu(\psi_1,E),\nu(\psi_2,E)\}
$$

for every prime divisor $E$ over $X$, so the maximum of two members has the
same divisorial profile $d$.

Put $U=(\sup_{\psi\in\mathcal F_d}\psi)^*$. By Choquet's lemma, choose a
sequence $\psi_j\in\mathcal F_d$ whose upper envelope is $U$, and replace it
by the increasing sequence $u_j=\max\{\psi_1,\ldots,\psi_j\}$. Thus each
$u_j$ has profile $d$ and $u_j\nearrow U$ almost everywhere.

We spell out the generic-divisor passage. Fix a model on which a prime divisor
$E$ occurs. Choose a very general point of $E$ simultaneously for the countable
family of pullbacks of the $u_j$ and for the pullback of $U$. Their generic
Lelong numbers are then their point Lelong numbers at that point. After adding
a smooth local potential, the pullbacks form an increasing sequence of psh
functions. The increasing-sequence Lelong theorem therefore gives

$$
\nu(U,E)=\lim_{j\to\infty}\nu(u_j,E)=\nu(d,E).
$$

The valuative multiplier-ideal criterion, applied after every positive integer
scaling, now gives $[U]_{\mathcal I}=d$. Hence $U\in\mathcal F_d$, and it is
the largest member of that family. The family depends only on $d$, so
$U=\mathcal R_\theta(d)$ and applying the construction again returns $U$.

Also $\sup_XU=0$: otherwise a sufficiently small positive constant could be
added without changing multiplier ideals, contradicting maximality in
$\mathcal F_d$. If $u$ is any normalized $\mathcal I$-model potential in the
class $d$, its defining competitor family is the same $\mathcal F_d$, and
fixedness gives $u=U$. This proves the first assertion.

For the second assertion, choose a compact generalized Cantor set
$F\subset\mathbf P^1$ with stage lengths $\ell_0=1$ and
$\ell_m=\exp(-4^m)$ for $m\ge1$. Since

$$
2\ell_1<\ell_0,\qquad
\frac{2\ell_{m+1}}{\ell_m}=2\exp(-3\cdot4^m)<1\quad(m\ge1),
$$

two child intervals fit at every stage. Give each stage-$m$ interval mass
$2^{-m}$. The resulting probability measure $\mu$ is nonatomic, and the
classical generalized-Cantor capacity criterion gives that $F$ is polar because

$$
\sum_{m\ge0}2^{-m}\log\frac1{\ell_m}
=\sum_{m\ge1}2^m=+\infty.
$$

Let $G_p$ be the normalized Green potential on $\mathbf P^1$ satisfying

$$
\omega+\operatorname{dd}^cG_p=\delta_p,\qquad \sup_XG_p=0,
$$

and put $G_\mu(z)=\int_XG_p(z)\,d\mu(p)$. It is not identically
$-\infty$: a point outside $F$ has positive chordal distance from $F$, which
gives a finite uniform lower bound for all integrands. Fubini's theorem yields

$$
\omega+\operatorname{dd}^cG_\mu=\mu.
$$

For $0\le s\le1$, let $\varphi_s=sG_\mu$. Then

$$
\omega+\operatorname{dd}^c\varphi_s=(1-s)\omega+s\mu.
$$

On a Riemann surface, the Lelong number of a positive $(1,1)$-current at a
point is its atomic mass. Both $\omega$ and $\mu$ are nonatomic, so all Lelong
numbers of $\varphi_s$ vanish. Since the prime divisors over a smooth curve are
its points, the valuative multiplier-ideal criterion applied to $m\varphi_s$
gives $\mathcal I(m\varphi_s)=\mathcal O_X$ for every $m\ge1$. Hence
$[\varphi_s]_{\mathcal I}=[0]_{\mathcal I}$.

The degree-one nonpluripolar product is local where the potential is locally
bounded and charges no pluripolar set. $G_\mu$ is locally bounded on
$X\setminus F$. Hence

$$
\mathbf1_{X\setminus F}\left\langle
  \omega+\operatorname{dd}^c\varphi_s\right\rangle
=(1-s)\mathbf1_{X\setminus F}\omega.
$$

The nonpluripolar product gives $F$ zero mass, and so does the smooth measure
$\omega$. Therefore

$$
\left\langle\omega+\operatorname{dd}^c\varphi_s\right\rangle=(1-s)\omega,
\qquad
\int_X\left\langle\omega+\operatorname{dd}^c\varphi_s\right\rangle=1-s.
$$

Applying the first assertion to their common class gives

$$
\mathcal R_\omega([\varphi_s]_{\mathcal I})
=\mathcal R_\omega([0]_{\mathcal I})=0.
$$

At $s=1$, the input representative has mass zero while its canonical
normalized $\mathcal I$-model has mass one. This proves the claimed
non-reconstruction.
